content.caseIdentity: Ashby v White, (1703) 2 Ld Raym 938; (1703) 92 ER 126
content.facts: Ashby, a qualified voter, was prevented from casting his vote at an election. The case is associated with the proposition that infringement of a legal right may constitute actionable injury even without proof of financial loss.
questionsBeforeCourt: Whether a qualified elector could maintain an action where his vote was wrongfully refused and no specific financial loss was shown.
content.ratioDecidendi: The case is a leading historical authority associated with injuria sine damno: infringement of a legal right may be actionable notwithstanding absence of consequential financial loss. The reported litigation and later treatment of Holt CJ's reasoning should be read with care when describing the precise procedural and remedial basis.
content.holding: The litigation concerned wrongful refusal of a qualified elector's vote and is commonly cited for the injuria sine damno principle.
content.relevance: Use this historical authority to illustrate legal injury without consequential financial loss; verify the precise procedural history and remedial proposition before relying on it for a specific modern cause of action.

evidence.note: English Court of Queen's Bench (1703) 2 Ld Raym 938; 92 ER 126; Holt CJ holding establishing injuria sine damno.

propositionVerification.rule: Authoritative evidence is attached as provenance. This phase does not rewrite, promote, or certify a proposition unless proposition-level legal review confirms the exact holding/ratio against the authoritative decision.
